title: Your AI problem is actually a network problem
summary: See how IT/OT convergence connects clean, accurate plant data to AI initiatives and discover the four network realities that can make or break AI’s success.
body_markdown:
It also changed what the plant can trust: with clean, isolated traffic, the maintenance and quality data that feeds future AI models will be more reliable and easier to validate.


For a North American material handling and logistics automation company, we’re turning vibration and current data into automatic service alerts to help their team catch a problem before it escalates rather than after. This anomaly detection works because network segmentation was done first: It gives vibration and current signals a dedicated, consistent path to travel so the system can distinguish a developing equipment problem from a network-related data issue.


### 3. The plant is never greenfield


A real plant environment rarely looks like the clean, uniform environment an AI initiative assumes. Instead, it operates on multiple protocols and multiple generations of equipment from different vendors. Machines on 15- to 30-year lifecycles share the same environment as IT systems that are refreshed every three to five years.


To support this mix, the **network must be designed for multi-vendor plant environments** , harmonizing what’s in place rather than forcing plants to standardize on one vendor and one standard.


We watched a **pharmaceutical manufacturer in the Middle East** connect roughly 500 nodes to a single resilient network despite significant site constraints. Network deployment was limited to areas outside hygiene zones, cabling access was restricted and equipment from different vendors used overlapping IP addresses. To work around those constraints, the plant network was divided into rings and sub-rings that maintain clear visibility into which device generates each data point.


At our own **century-old Richmond, IN, facility** , poor visibility contributed to frequent unplanned downtime, disconnected legacy equipment and limited ability to see problems as they happened. Rather than replace our legacy equipment to modernize, we connected it—regardless of age—to a single, secure, vendor-neutral network and layered in real-time sensing to improve production visibility and responsiveness.


### 4. Convergence depends on more than technology


The costliest convergence failures are organizational, not technical. Convergence forces three groups into the same room:


- **IT** wants to extend governance into the plant
- **Security** wants control
- **OT** wants uptime and no one to touch the control loop


Each is right on its own terms, and each is incomplete alone. Projects freeze in the gap that exists between them.


These teams don’t always work effectively together, either: In Palo Alto Networks’ *[2024 State of OT Security](https://www.paloaltonetworks.com/resources/research/state-of-ot-security-report)* survey of nearly 2,000 industrial leaders, 40% describe the relationship between IT and OT as “frictional,” and only 12% call it “aligned.”
